strengths: Addresses an important and persistent problem in text-to-image diffusion: missing, merged, or imbalanced concepts in compositional prompts.

The proposed sampler is training-free, gradient-free, and does not depend on attention-map access, making it practically attractive and more architecture-independent than many optimization-based alternatives.
Results on SDXL are promising, especially for animal–animal and animal–object prompts, and the paper compares against several relevant compositional-generation methods.
The component ablations, runtime comparison, hyperparameter sweeps, qualitative failure cases, and preliminary PixArt-Σ examples provide useful supporting evidence.
The manuscript is generally understandable and explicitly discusses limitations and broader societal risks.
weaknesses: The central probabilistic justification is not sound. The ratio p_t(x|C)^w0 divided by products of p_t(x|c_k) with negative exponents is not guaranteed to be normalizable and can assign extreme mass where a denominator is small. Consequently, it need not define the claimed corrector distribution or preferentially select images where all concepts coexist.

The theoretical results are largely algebraic constraints on a chosen parameterization, not guarantees of valid diffusion sampling. In particular, any vector can formally be written as x−sigma*epsilon, while preservation of a CFG-shaped expression does not establish that the resulting epsilon is the score of a valid forward-diffused distribution. The same marginal-consistency issue used to criticize composable diffusion remains unresolved here.

The implemented algorithm further departs from the claimed distributional interpretation through norm-based Tweedie-mean rescaling and repeated off-trajectory updates. No derivation shows that these operations sample Equation 12. The resampler is explicitly acknowledged to be theoretically valid only at the initial noise step but is nevertheless applied at later steps.

The mode-overlap hypothesis is not directly tested. Figure 2 is insufficiently specified—sample size, prompts, variability, and precise protocol are missing—and metric improvements alone do not establish that overlap with individual-concept modes caused the failures or that CO3 suppresses such overlap.

The evaluation omits essential statistical information: numbers of prompts and generated samples, seed matching, confidence intervals, significance tests, and per-prompt variability are not reported. Reliance only on BLIP-VQA and ImageReward, without human evaluation or more targeted binding/counting metrics, is especially limiting for qualitative compositional claims.

Several headline comparisons are confounded by different base models: multiple baselines use SD1.5 whereas CO3 uses SDXL. Among SDXL methods, CO3 is not consistently best—for example, ToMe has substantially higher object-category BLIP-VQA—and the PixArt-Σ generalization evidence is qualitative and apparently based on a few selected prompts.

Claims about complex prompts and arbitrary numbers of concepts are supported only by a small qualitative figure; the quantitative benchmark is restricted to mostly two-concept prompts. There is no scaling analysis with concept count, relation complexity, parser failures, or difficult negation/counting cases.

CO3 costs about 19.9 seconds per sample versus 7.2 seconds for SDXL, nearly a threefold slowdown, despite being described as lightweight. Quality–runtime tradeoffs and comparisons under matched compute are not studied.

Reproducibility is incomplete within the manuscript: important evaluation and sampling details are missing, notation for guidance/correction weights is inconsistent across the main text and appendix, and some reported baseline values differ across tables. Overall, the empirical idea is promising, but the unsupported theoretical interpretation and inconclusive evaluation keep the submission below the top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and persistent problem in text-to-image diffusion: dropped, merged, or imbalanced concepts in compositional prompts.
CO3 is training-free, gradient-free, and broadly compatible with pretrained denoisers. The hybrid resampling/correction procedure is conceptually simple and potentially useful in practice.
The experiments include several relevant baselines, two automatic metrics, component ablations, inference-time measurements, qualitative failure cases, and demonstrations on both SDXL and PixArt-Σ.
The reported SDXL results are encouraging in the animal–animal and animal–object categories, particularly under ImageReward.
weaknesses: The central probabilistic formulation is internally inconsistent. Equation 12 divides by concept densities raised to weights that are subsequently required to be negative; this mathematically multiplies rather than suppresses those densities. More generally, dividing by single-concept densities can favor low-density or semantically irrelevant regions, and the paper provides no conditions ensuring that the proposed ratio is normalizable or corresponds to the claimed “pure” modes.

The theoretical contribution is substantially overstated. A weighted combination failing to retain one particular CFG parameterization does not imply that it is not a valid Tweedie mean or diffusion update: any resulting noise vector defines a Tweedie estimate, and composable guidance can be reparameterized using an aggregate guidance scale and normalized conditional combination. The lemmas establish elementary algebraic identities, not correctness of the sampler or superiority over score-space composition.

The mode-overlap hypothesis is never tested directly. Improved benchmark scores do not establish that failures arise from overlapping modes or that CO3 removes such modes, so repeated claims of empirical validation are unsupported.

The quantitative evaluation is not sufficiently rigorous. The manuscript omits prompt counts, numbers of seeds or generated samples, uncertainty estimates, statistical tests, and human evaluation. BLIP-VQA and ImageReward alone are inadequate for verifying multi-object presence, attribute binding, spatial relations, and perceptual quality, particularly because ImageReward mixes alignment with aesthetics.

Baseline comparisons are difficult to interpret: results from SD1.5 and SDXL are presented together, the details and tuning of adapted SDXL baselines are limited, and the strongest claims for PixArt-Σ and complex prompts rely only on selected qualitative examples. There is also no quantitative comparison with the closely related TweedieMix approach.

Reproducibility details conflict. The main text specifies CFG scale λ=5.0, whereas appendix sweeps use λ=0.8 or 0.9 without clearly introducing a different parameter; reported SDXL baseline values also differ between Tables 1 and 2. The scale or normalization of the high-dimensional distance used inside exp(-βd) is unspecified, raising numerical and implementation questions.

The ablation is cumulative rather than factorial and shows that adding the corrector after resampling decreases several individual scores, making its distinct benefit unclear. Hyperparameters appear extensively swept on the evaluation benchmark, with no validation/test separation described.

The method is not especially lightweight in practice: reported inference time rises from 7.2 seconds for SDXL to 19.9 seconds for CO3. This substantial cost, together with only modest BLIP-VQA gains over SDXL in two categories, weakens the practical significance claim.

Prompt decomposition removes adjectives and retains nouns, which narrows the mechanism and leaves its behavior on attributes, relations, parsing errors, repeated entities, and genuinely many-concept prompts poorly characterized. Overall, the empirical signal is promising, but the theoretical flaws and incomplete evaluation prevent acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper proposes a useful training-free and gradient-free sampler for improving multi-concept generation, with a simple plug-and-play design that does not depend on attention maps or model-specific architecture.
The hybrid combination of early noise resampling, subsequent latent correction, and closeness-aware weighting is intuitively motivated and practically interesting.
On the standard compositional benchmark, CO3 obtains strong SDXL results, leading the compared SDXL methods on most reported BLIP-VQA and ImageReward categories.
The experimental section includes competitive baselines, component ablations, hyperparameter sweeps, qualitative failure cases, runtime measurements, and qualitative transfer to PixArt-Sigma.
The paper is generally understandable and discusses limitations, reproducibility, and broader impacts.
weaknesses: The central theoretical presentation has a serious sign inconsistency: Eq. 12 divides by individual-concept densities raised to weights w_k, while Eqs. 13-15 specify negative w_k. Taken literally, these definitions induce opposite effects, so the stated distribution and implemented composition do not match.

The sum-to-one argument is overstated. A composable-diffusion expression with weights lambda_k can be rewritten in CFG form using aggregate guidance L=sum_k lambda_k and normalized conditional weights lambda_k/L. Thus, sum-to-one is needed to preserve the same fixed guidance scale under the paper's parameterization, but not to establish CFG representability or validity in the broader sense claimed. Moreover, an affine vector estimate is not automatically the score or Tweedie mean of a normalized diffusion distribution.

The mode-overlap hypothesis is not directly tested. Improved learned-metric scores do not establish that problematic modes arise from density overlap or that CO3 selects the claimed pure joint modes; the likelihood-ratio distribution may also be non-normalizable or emphasize low-density regions.

The evaluation relies almost entirely on BLIP-VQA and ImageReward, without human evaluation, sample counts, variance across seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. This is especially limiting because several gains are modest and learned metrics can share biases with the evaluated generators.

Several comparisons conflate the sampling method with the backbone: many baselines use SD1.5 while CO3 uses SDXL. Transfer to PixArt-Sigma and performance on genuinely complex prompts are only shown through a small, potentially cherry-picked qualitative set.

Claims of extension to arbitrary numbers of concepts and complex relations are insufficiently supported. The tested quantitative benchmark is narrow, and the noun parser explicitly removes adjectives even though attribute binding is part of the claimed capability.

Reproducibility details are internally inconsistent or unclear: the main text describes a 5.0 guidance scale and correction over the first 20% of 50 steps, whereas appendix sweeps use lambda values of 0.8-0.9 and varying num_ts; the meanings and interaction of these parameters are not adequately reconciled.

CO3 takes 19.9 seconds versus 7.2 seconds for base SDXL, roughly a 2.8-fold slowdown, yet the paper describes the guidance as lightweight and does not analyze memory or scaling cost as the number of concepts grows.

strengths: Addresses an important and persistent problem in text-to-image generation with a plug-and-play, training-free, gradient-free sampling method.

Reports encouraging improvements over SDXL across several compositional benchmarks, with useful ablations, PixArt generalization, low-step and DPM++ experiments, runtime/memory measurements, and qualitative failure cases.
The hybrid resampling/correction design and closeness-aware weighting are intuitive and practically relevant.
The paper is generally well organized and includes pseudocode, implementation settings, a reproducibility statement, and broader-impact discussion.
weaknesses: The central theoretical justification is not sound as stated. The unit-sum result only shows preservation of a particular fixed-scale CFG parameterization; it does not establish that other compositions are invalid Tweedie means or lack a coherent distribution. In particular, composable-diffusion guidance can be rewritten using a rescaled global guidance factor and normalized weights, undermining the claimed explanation for its failures.

Equation 12 is internally inconsistent with the algorithm: individual-concept terms appear in the denominator while their weights are later defined as negative, which would strengthen rather than suppress those concepts. Moreover, quotients involving negative density powers need not be normalizable. Mean normalization and unconditional-manifold correction further depart from the proposed distribution without theoretical analysis.

The evaluation lacks essential statistical detail: numbers of prompts and generated samples are not reported, variability over seeds and confidence intervals are absent, and the 11-person human study does not specify assignments, sample counts, inter-rater agreement, or significance testing.

Several empirical claims overstate the tables. CO3 is not uniformly best or tied on T2ICompBench/RareBench: it is below other methods on RareBench Relations ImageReward and below SDXL on RareBench Complex human evaluation. Baselines also mix SD1.5 and SDXL configurations, limiting some comparisons.

There are material reproducibility inconsistencies. Table 8 labels SDXL as 50-step but reports the same scores as the 10-step SDXL row in Table 7; the main setup uses guidance scale 5.0 while appendix sweeps use 0.8–0.9 without clearly distinguishing the quantities; and some human-evaluation baseline entries are missing.

The practical cost is substantial despite the lightweight framing: 50-step CO3 is about 2.8 times slower than SDXL and slower than ToMe. The paper does not compare quality at matched wall-clock or model-call budgets.

Overall, the empirical idea is promising, but the flawed/overstated theory and insufficiently controlled evaluation prevent the submission from meeting the technical-soundness standard of a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper targets an important and persistent problem in text-to-image diffusion: missing, merged, or imbalanced concepts in compositional prompts.
CO3 is training-free, gradient-free, and largely architecture-independent. Avoiding backward passes gives it a practical memory advantage over attention-optimization methods.

The empirical scope is reasonably broad: two diffusion backbones, several compositional and rare-concept benchmarks, multiple automatic metrics, a human evaluation, component ablations, low-step and alternative-solver experiments, and runtime/memory measurements.

Several reported improvements over the corresponding base models are substantial, especially on Animal–Animal prompts. The ablations suggest that resampling, correction, and adaptive weighting each contribute.
The paper acknowledges failure cases and potential misuse of improved image generation.
weaknesses: The central probabilistic formulation is internally inconsistent. Equation 12 places p(x_t|c_k)^{w_k} in the denominator while defining w_k<0; this mathematically multiplies by positive powers of the individual-concept distributions, contrary to the stated suppression objective and the negative-weight composition in Equation 13.

The main theoretical result does not justify the paper's strong claims. The unit-sum condition is essentially an affine-algebra identity needed to retain a particular CFG parameterization. It does not establish that the composed prediction is the score of a coherent joint distribution, that it follows the appropriate diffusion forward process, or that it samples from Equation 12. In the unrestricted sense, any vector can be written as x_t−σ_t epsilon, so the claimed 'if and only if' validity of a Tweedie mean is misleading.

Consequently, the proposed mode-overlap explanation remains speculative. No density, mode-overlap, trajectory, or controlled synthetic analysis directly tests whether failures arise from overlap with single-concept distributions. Improved benchmark scores do not by themselves validate this causal hypothesis.

Several conclusions overstate the results. CO3 does not consistently outperform or match the best baseline in Table 2: on RareBench Relations, its ImageReward score (0.2588) is below SDXL (0.3607) and R2F (0.3620), and on RareBench Complex its human score (0.6117) is below SDXL (0.6283). It also trails several methods on some Table 1 categories and metrics.

The quantitative reporting contains concerning inconsistencies. Table 8 labels an SDXL result as 50-step sampling but reports exactly the much weaker 10-step numbers from Table 7, exaggerating the apparent quality gap in the efficiency comparison. SDXL values also differ between Tables 1 and 3, and the main text states CFG lambda=5 while appendix hyperparameter studies use lambda=0.8–0.9 without clearly reconciling the definitions or identifying the final selected configuration.

The evaluation lacks statistical support. The manuscript provides no sample counts per benchmark result, variance across seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. This is particularly problematic because diffusion outputs and learned metrics are noisy and many reported differences are small.

The human study is insufficiently documented: only 11 participants are reported, with no number of evaluated prompts/images, assignment scheme, per-image rating count, inter-rater agreement, uncertainty, significance analysis, or clear explanation for missing baseline entries. Side-by-side presentation may also create comparative dependencies that are not analyzed.

Baseline fairness is uneven. Table 1 mixes SD1.5-based methods with an SDXL-based proposed method, some baselines are selectively adapted or stripped of components, and the harder-benchmark comparison retains only a small subset of competitors. There is no comparison to simple negative-prompt or score-subtraction controls that would help isolate the novelty of the proposed construction.

The method is not especially lightweight computationally: five correction iterations requiring several conditional denoiser evaluations make 50-step CO3 about 2.8 times slower than base SDXL (19.90 versus 7.20 seconds). The quality–compute tradeoff is not compared under equal latency or equal numbers of network evaluations.

Reproducibility is weaker than claimed. The abstract's code link is blank, important benchmark/sample-count details are absent, automatic concept extraction discards adjectives despite evaluating attribute binding, and the manuscript does not explain failures of parsing or handling of relations and more complex noun phrases.

Qualitative examples are selectively chosen and frequently shift toward sparse, stylized, or illustration-like outputs. There is no blinded large-scale assessment of visual quality, diversity, background fidelity, or degradation relative to the base model. Given the central theoretical errors and unreliable reporting, the promising empirical idea is not sufficiently substantiated for acceptance.

strengths: CO3 is a practically relevant, training-free, gradient-free approach to multi-concept text-to-image generation. The hybrid use of early resampling, later correction, and adaptive concept weights is intuitive and straightforward to integrate into existing samplers.

The empirical study is unusually broad: it covers SDXL and PixArt, multiple compositional and rare-concept benchmarks, automated metrics, human evaluation, component and hyperparameter ablations, qualitative examples, low-step and higher-order solvers, failure cases, and runtime/memory measurements.

Several improvements are substantial, especially for animal–animal prompts, DINOv2 concept recognition, and human ratings on the Attend-and-Excite benchmark. The PixArt results also provide useful evidence that the method is not tied to one architecture.
The paper is generally readable, motivates a recognizable failure mode, supplies pseudocode and implementation details, and discusses computational cost and broader impacts.
weaknesses: The central mode-overlap hypothesis is not directly tested. Improved prompt alignment does not establish that failures arise from overlapping probability modes or that CO3 reaches the claimed “pure” modes; no density, score-landscape, or overlap analysis is presented.

The theoretical framing is substantially overstated. Under the unit-sum constraint, linear composition of Tweedie means algebraically reduces to linear composition of predicted noises, so it is unclear in what substantive sense this departs from score composition. Moreover, satisfying the affine unit-sum condition does not by itself show that the resulting vector is the score or Tweedie mean of a coherent, normalizable conditional distribution. The proposition’s “if and only if” language is only defensible under a much narrower, fixed-CFG parameterization than stated.

Equation 12 has an apparent sign inconsistency: the individual distributions occur in the denominator while their weights are declared negative, which would reinforce rather than suppress them. This conflicts with Equation 1 and the later negative-weight construction.

Several empirical claims are stronger than the tables support. For example, CO3 does not match or outperform all methods across every Table 2 category and metric: it trails SDXL/R2F on Relations ImageReward and trails SDXL on RareBench-Complex human evaluation. Results on object–object prompts are also mixed.

Evaluation reporting lacks the sample counts, number of generated images per prompt, uncertainty estimates, significance tests, and sufficiently detailed human-study allocation needed to judge robustness. Eleven participants alone does not resolve this, especially without confidence intervals or inter-rater analysis.

Baseline comparability is imperfect: Table 1 mixes SD1.5- and SDXL-based methods, some methods are reimplemented or modified, and CO3 uses many additional denoiser evaluations. A compute-matched comparison such as repeated sampling or best-of-N selection is missing.

There are notable reporting inconsistencies. Most seriously, Table 8 labels the SDXL row as 50 steps but reports the same quality values as the 10-step DDIM baseline in Table 7, undermining that efficiency comparison. Other numerical discrepancies appear between tables as well.

The evidence for model agnosticism remains limited to one additional model and mostly the same simple benchmark; broader testing on modern diffusion/flow backbones and more challenging relation or counting prompts would strengthen the claim.
